extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (especially those writing characters from cultures other than their own)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for fiction authors on how to read and write characters from cultures different than their own while avoiding cultural appropriation, through sensitivity, deep character work, research, and outside feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yes! to greater sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Challenge yourself to question the information you're given and where it comes from, and be more sensitive about what could be insulting to others and why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expecting more of ourselves leads us to become more discerning readers, writers and people. Increasing sensitivity is framed as both necessary and beneficial: it improves storytelling and interpersonal understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writers have license to create diverse characters (with responsibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: All writers need license to create characters from different races, backgrounds and cultures; freedom to imagine is fundamental to creating art and meeting readers' interest in diverse stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While authors should feel free to imagine people unlike themselves, that freedom carries the responsibility to take character development seriously and avoid careless or exploitative portrayals. Example works are cited where the author wrote characters of different origins respectfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental respect for each character
rubrics_metrics.description: Create each character not as a type (e.g., store clerk, servant, villain) but as a real person with real dreams, flaws, and conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respectful character creation allows curiosity to reach beyond surface markers (color, race, ethnicity, gender) into deeper fears and motivations. The article uses the protagonist Pino as an example of a fully realized character with personal stakes and history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dive deeply into a character's reality through research
rubrics_metrics.description: Research what a character says and does and why — investigate their reality to avoid clichés, myths, and incorrect information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thorough, focused research into a character’s cultural, historical, and social context helps authors bypass stereotypes and inaccuracies. Research should inform specific details of speech, behavior, belief, and context rather than relying on broad generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every author has blind spots — actively find and resolve them
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should purposefully search for information that identifies and obliterates their blind spots and biases, because even well-intentioned writers carry absorbed unfair messages or systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledging that you may not be unbiased is a precondition to improving portrayals. Actively seek sources that challenge your assumptions and expose hidden prejudices rather than only confirming what you already believe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ sensitivity readers and diverse media to catch oversights
rubrics_metrics.description: Use sensitivity readers, articles, videos, podcasts and other perspectives to point out what authors might have overlooked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensitivity readers can reveal issues invisible to the author; the author describes a project where a sensitivity reader dramatically changed the team's understanding. Combine formal readers with varied media sources for a broader check on representation.
